1	# jj and cross-repo linking
2	
3	How version control is driven on this project (jj, never raw git) and how the two repos'
4	commits point at each other (the `ochid:` trailer). Read this before any jj operation beyond
5	`st` / `log` / `diff`, and always before touching a commit description.
6	
7	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
8	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
9	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## jj Basics
12	
13	**Use jj, not git, for version-control operations** (status, log, diff, commit, push, history
14	rewrite). jj coexists with the git backend, so the repo *can* be driven with raw `git`, but
15	this project's workflow (bookmarks, the working-copy `@` model, ochid trailers) is expressed in
16	jj terms. Reaching for `git` invites state that doesn't match the jj documentation here. There
17	is no `jj mv`: to move/rename a tracked file, just `mv` it on disk and jj detects the rename by
18	content.
19	
20	- `jj st -R .` / `jj st -R .claude`: show working copy status
21	- `jj log -R .` / `jj log -R .claude`: show commit log
22	- `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: finalize working copy into a commit
23	- `jj describe -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: set description without committing
24	- `jj git push --bookmark <name> -R <repo>`: push a bookmark (no `--allow-new` flag: jj pushes
25	  new bookmarks without special flags)
26	- `jj bookmark set <name> -r <rev> -R <repo>`: create the bookmark, or move an existing one, at
27	  `<rev>`. Moving it backwards needs `--allow-backwards`
28	- `jj git push --named <name>=<rev> -R <repo>`: create *and* publish in one step, which is the
29	  usual way a cycle's bookmark is born (see [Cycle bookmarks](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land))
30	- In jj, the working copy (@) is always a mutable commit being edited. `jj commit` finalizes it
31	  and creates a new empty working copy on top.
32	- The agent repo always has uncommitted changes during an active session because session data
33	  updates continuously.
34	- `jj rebase` uses `--onto`/`-o` to name the destination(s).
35	
36	Viewing, for a review: `jj diff -R .` is the working copy, `jj diff -r @- -R .` the previous
37	commit, `jj show -r <X> -R .` one revision's description and diff. Never `jj edit -r @-` to view
38	a past commit: it marks it mutable and shifts `@`.
39	
40	## Revsets
41	
42	How commits are addressed in `-r` arguments, condensed. jj's own semantics are the one dialect.
43	The full language is `jj help -k revsets`, the single authority, and the worked tutorial with
44	terminal transcripts is `jj-tips.md`, hosted once in the template repository.
45	
46	- A revision is `@` (the working copy), a chid prefix, or a commit id. Unambiguous prefixes
47	  are accepted, and ambiguous ones are rejected, never guessed.
48	- Neighbors: `@-` parent, `@--` grandparent, `@+` child. A step past the end of the chain is
49	  the empty set, not an error.
50	- `::` is the primary range operator, symmetric and endpoint-inclusive:
51	  - `::x` ancestors of x, including x. `x::` descendants of x, including x
52	  - `x::y` the DAG path: descendants of x that are also ancestors of y
53	- `..` is git-compatible set subtraction, not a tighter `::`:
54	  - `x..y` is `::y ~ ::x`: ancestors of y that are not ancestors of x
55	  - `x..` is `~::x`: every visible commit that is not an ancestor of x. Open-ended, so on a repo
56	    with parked branches it includes commits unrelated to x
57	  - `..x` is `::x ~ root()`: ancestors of x, excluding the root
58	- Useful sets: `jj log` (default revset), `jj log -r ::@` (all ancestors of `@`),
59	  `jj log -r 'all()'` (all visible commits), `jj evolog -r X` (one change's rewrite history),
60	  `jj op log` (operation history).
61	
62	History note: an earlier house convention glossed `x..` as "descendants of x excluding x", which
63	is not jj's meaning. Old transcripts and notes written under that gloss decode against it.
64	Durable text written since teaches only jj's semantics.
65	
66	## Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)
67	
68	The cross-reference between the work repo and the agent repo is what makes the dual-repo work:
69	every commit points at its counterpart in the other repo, so the "what" (code) and the
70	"why / how" (session) stay linked across time. That pointer is the **ochid** (Other Change ID)
71	git trailer.
72	
73	A **chid** is jj's change ID, a permanent identifier that survives rebases and `describe`s
74	(unlike the commit ID / git SHA, which changes on rewrite). An **ochid** trailer carries the
75	counterpart commit's chid as a workspace-root-relative path:
76	
77	- Paths start with `/`, the workspace root, i.e. the work repo (the project root). `/.claude`
78	  is the agent sub-repo.
79	- `ochid: /<chid>` references a change in the **work repo**.
80	- `ochid: /.claude/<chid>` references a change in the **agent repo**.
81	
82	Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value` lines at the end of the commit body, using the
83	chid's **12-character** prefix:
84	
85	```
86	ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqowktp   # points to an agent-repo change
87	ochid: /wtpmottvxqzl           # points to a work-repo change
88	```
89	
90	How many, and which direction:
91	
92	- **Work-repo commits** each carry one `ochid: /.claude/<agent-chid>`, the agent repo's change ID.
93	- **The agent-repo commit** carries one `ochid: /<work-chid>` per work-repo commit in that push.
94	  The count is per *push*, not per cycle. A trapezoid close-out whose rungs were pushed 1:1 as
95	  they landed still carries exactly one. More than one occurs when a single push publishes
96	  several work-repo commits.
97	
98	Use `vc-x1 chid -s work,agent -L` to capture the change IDs (first line work repo, second agent
99	repo).
100	
101	`ochid:` trailers are **stamped by `vc-x1 push`**. Never hand-write them into a commit body or
102	`--title`/`--body`.
103	
104	## vc-x1 push: what it does and does not do
105	
106	`vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."` commits both repos with the approved title
107	and body, stamps each new commit's `ochid:` trailer ([above](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)),
108	pushes the work bookmark, and squash-pushes the agent repo's `main`. Three behaviors to keep in
109	mind:
110	
111	- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 runs no build or tests. Validation is the per-rung
112	  flow's job, run *before* the push. The one check that remains is `push-work` verifying the
113	  bookmark's remote refs are tracked.
114	- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume: every stage no-ops when its
115	  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If push exits after `push-work`
116	  but before the agent-repo publish, `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` by hand is the rest of it.
117	- **`ochid:` trailers are stamped by push** (hard rule 5), never hand-written into `--title` or
118	  `--body`.
119	
120	A late work-repo tweak after the push (a forgotten edit) needs `jj squash --ignore-immutable`
121	and a re-push, which is a remote rewrite and takes approval like any push.
122	
123	## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer
124	
125	**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
126	coordinating with everyone involved first.** It is a history rewrite, and it silently drops the
127	cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been described and carries no
128	trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not covered. That is a
129	[local ladder](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders)'s scratch describe.
130	
131	When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
132	hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one
133	already stamped). Hit at a coordinated amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that
134	way. `vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.

Reviewed. The two-mode split (one commit at a time, then a range) is a real improvement: my version buried the range form in a trailing sentence, and separating them makes both readable. Findings, worst first.

**1. Three broken links.** `[New version](#new-version)`, `[Old version](#old-version)` and `[Diff](#diff)` point at headings that do not exist. The three views are bold leads inside a bullet list, so markdown generates no anchors for them. All three links dead-end. Either drop the link syntax and name them plainly, or promote the three views to `###` headings, which changes the section's shape.

**2. A sentence is missing its noun.** "you are viewing the squash commit of the ([Close-out shapes](#close-out-shapes))" has a dangling "of the". Also, "squash commit" names a commit that does not exist yet at the moment the reader is looking, so "what a squash would carry" is the accurate phrase.

**3. Misplaced parenthesis.** "to the longest file's length or a large number like (`--context 1000` is the CLI equivalent)" reads as "a large number like (parenthetical)". The number itself fell out: "a large number such as 1000 (`--context 1000` is the CLI equivalent)".

**4. Two typos.** "look at a one commit at a time" and "Hover over the any commit above".

**5. One line is 101 cols**, the "Diff marked commit" bullet, one over the 100 limit.

**6. Backticks inside a quoted UI label.** `"Diff marked commit -> `this`"` puts markup inside what claims to be gitk's menu text verbatim. gitk's label has no backticks.

**7. Voice, your call.** The new paragraph carries five of jj.md's seven second-person usages; the file is otherwise impersonal. There is precedent (two pre-existing), so this is a preference, not an error.

With 1 through 6 applied, keeping your voice and structure:

> Raise "Lines of context" to the longest file's length, or to a large number such as 1000 (`--context 1000` is the CLI equivalent), to see the entire file, then select:
>
> [the three bullets unchanged]
>
> The above reads one commit at a time and is useful. Another mode is to see how several commits together changed the tree since a given `<base>`. To do that:
>
> - Hover over the commit you want as the `<base>`, right click and select "Mark this commit".
> - Hover over any commit above the `<base>`, right click and select "Diff marked commit -> this".
>
> Now New version, Old version and Diff show the net change of everything between `<base>` and `this`. If `<base>` is the parent of the opening and `this` is the closing, that is what a squash of the cycle would carry, and it can help you decide what shape to choose ([Close-out shapes](#close-out-shapes)).

The plain version: the structure you added is better than what I wrote, but the three view links point at headings that do not exist, one sentence lost its noun after "of the", and the context sentence lost the number it was meant to suggest. Everything else is typos and one over-long line.

gitk renders a change three ways, and at full context each answers a different question. Raise
"Lines of context" to the longest file's length or a large number like (`--context 1000` is the
CLI equivalent) to see the entire file, then select:

- **New version**: the file as it now is, with the added lines lit. This is what the permanent
  branch will carry, so it is the view for judging whether a change reads as one thing.
- **Old version**: the file as it was, with the removed lines lit. It answers what the change
  costs, which a diff states only as minus lines out of context.
- **Diff**: the two interleaved. At full context it is the whole file with the edit marked in
  place, which is the reading a reviewer wants when the edit is small and the file is not.

The above allows you to look at a one commit at a time and is useful. But another mode is to
look at how multiple commits changed a particular `<base>` commit. To do these two actions:
- Hover over the commit you like to be the `<base>`, right click and select "Mark this commit"
- Hover over the any commit above the `<base>`, right click and select "Diff marked commit -> `this`"

Now clicking on the [New version](#new-version), [Old version](#old-version) or [Diff](#diff)
you'll see the net change of everything between `<base>` and `this`. If `<base>` is the parent
of the `opening` commit and `this` is the `closing` you are viewing the squash commit of the
([Close-out shapes](#close-out-shapes)) and it can help you decide what shape to choose.

## Todo

 Entries are in **strict priority rank**, #1 highest,
 descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
 `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run TODO.md` to renumber.
 The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs, so to refer
 to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention,
 since a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
 number. Long-tail entries
 live in [todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the
 [Prose form](/agent-data/prose.md#prose-form). Deeper
 detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
 subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. Change hard rule "8. Typeable punctuation:" to "8. Prose style:" and include not only the
   "Typeable punctuation" but also no wall-of-prose. Instead use intro, bullet/sub-bullets.
2. **The agent-files are the proposal, custom.md the users' override.** (wink, 2026-08-23)
   The agent-files define a default set that others adopt as-is, modify, or override through
   custom.md. The family dogfoods the set as its first users, so a family member wanting a
   change edits the agent-files directly, the diff against the payload being the proposal,
   and its own custom.md stays the payload default. Overrides are for users of the set, not
   its authors.
   - restate AGENTS.md's "custom.md: the project layer" section and its rationale.md entry to
     this model, custom.md and precedence kept for downstream users (the content relocation
     itself was done at the reshape-at-land cycle's empty-custom.md rung)
3. **Fix `vc-x1 config`'s rendering: print once, and write with `--output`.** (wink, 2026-08-21)
   Bare `vc-x1 config` prints the schema once per side of the default `work,agent` target, and
   since every remaining key has both workspace homes the two blocks are identical apart from
   the header, so the reader sees the same ~40 lines twice. In a workspace with no agent side
   the second block is still printed, under the `<root>/<agent-dir>/...` fallback hint, for a
   side that does not exist.
   - print the schema once by default, grouped per side only when the sides' key sets differ
     (they will again once `[family]` and `[validate]` land as `workspace-code`-only)
   - add `--output <scope>:<path>[,<scope>:<path>]` or some such, writing each side's rendering
     to a file instead of stdout, so a side's config can be (re)generated in place. This
     overlaps `config --refresh` in "Finish the vc-config surface" and should be designed with
     it, one verb or two
   - skip a side the workspace does not have, rather than rendering its fallback hint
   - accept a directory as a path target (wink, 2026-08-21): `config --validate .claude` or
     `../iiac-perf` resolves through the carrier lookup (`config_md::vc_config_path`) to that
     side's config file, the both-carriers error included, and the report labels the side by
     the directory. Today a path target must name the file itself
   - an explicit path must exist (wink, 2026-08-21). Today `config xyz` prints the whole schema
     for "any home" with the path as a label and never opens it, and `config --validate xyz`
     reports the file "not found, skipping" and passes with zero problems, so a typo'd path

content.text:
Both are convention work, so both are their own cycle after this one closes. Here is what I found looking at each.

## Todo #1: hard rule 8 becomes "Prose style"

**The diagnosis is not that the rule is missing.** prose.md's Prose form already says it, in as many words: "Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they hide the structure that bullets make scannable." And the Conventional-commit shape section is explicit for the exact surface that failed: ladder details are "bulleted, never `;`-joined inline". The rule existed through all five rungs that ignored it.

So what failed is reach, not content. That points at two fixes with different leverage:

- **Promote it into the hard rules**, as you propose. The hard rules are the one list read at session start, so a rule there gets seen without anyone deciding to open prose.md.
- **Name the form at the point of action.** Per-rung flow step 4 currently says "write what this rung changed, conceptually, into its subsection". It never says what shape. Rule 7 exists precisely because the step is what gets read at the moment of writing, and step 4 is where I would have caught this. This is the fix I would weight higher.

I would do both, and I would take your rename.

**One caution on broadening rule 8.** The hard rules are numbered so a review can name one. Today "rule 8" resolves to a single mechanically-checkable thing: no em dash, en dash, ellipsis or arrow characters, which a byte scan finds. Folding in "no wall-of-prose" puts a judgment call under the same number, so "you broke rule 8" stops being unambiguous and a checker can only enforce half of it. That is survivable if the rule names its two halves so a review can say "rule 8, wall-of-prose", but it is a real change in kind and worth deciding deliberately rather than absorbing. The alternative is a rule 14 of its own, which keeps each number resolving to one thing.

## The hyphenation question

I counted across `AGENTS.md`, `custom.md` and `agent-data/*`. Three of the four apparent inconsistencies are not inconsistencies:

- **`closeout`**, 9 hits, is entirely `<closeout>`, the metavariable in jj.md's recipe. It is code, exempt like the semicolon rule's code allowance. Nothing to fix.
- **`at-rest` vs `At rest`**, 6 and 4, is correct English, not drift: `at-rest` is the compound modifier ("the at-rest contract"), `At rest` is the section name. Nothing to fix.
- **`change ID` vs `change id`**, 5 and 3, is capitalization, not hyphenation. Worth normalizing in the sweep, but it is a different question.

**The real one is the repo names**, and it is a rule violation rather than an open question:

| term | hyphenated | not |
|---|---|---|
| work-repo | 12 | 6 |
| agent-repo | 14 | 7 |

AGENTS.md's Terminology already decides this: *"Repos: the two repos of the dual-repo model, written hyphenated: 'work-repo', 'agent-repo'."* So 13 sites are simply wrong, most of them in jj.md's Cross-repo linking section.

Before sweeping, though, the rule deserves one honest look, because standard English would hyphenate only the modifier: "work-repo commits" but "the work repo". jj.md line 92 does exactly that, correctly, and reads better for it. Two coherent policies:

- **Always hyphenate**, the current rule. These are the proper names of two specific repos, it matches `agent-files` (hyphenated on the same argument: it names one set, not a two-word phrase) and its sibling directory `agent-data/`, and it is the only version a checker can enforce, a bare grep expecting zero outside code spans.
- **Hyphenate as a modifier only**, standard English. Reads more naturally in predicate position, but needs judgment at every site and cannot be checked.

I recommend keeping the current rule. The cheapest path is bringing 13 sites to a rule that already exists, and the enforceability argument is the same one that makes the semicolon rule work. The cost is admitted: "in the work-repo" reads slightly stiff, and `agent-files` already paid that price.

## Sequencing

Both are convention cycles, so neither starts before this one lands. They could be one cycle, since both are agent-file prose conventions, but the sweep is mechanical and delegatable while the rule change is not, so I would keep them separate.

One more convention itch to file so it does not get lost: rationale.md's How-to-read list has "a boundary sentence is not rationale" but not its sibling "a definition is not rationale", which is the rule that justified this cycle's three Terminology deletions and would stop someone re-adding them.

The plain version: for #1, the rule already existed in prose.md and was ignored, so promoting it to the hard rules is right but fixing per-rung flow step 4 matters more, and be deliberate about one number covering two different kinds of rule. For hyphenation, most of the apparent mess is not mess, and the one real case is 13 sites disagreeing with a rule AGENTS.md already states, so it is a sweep rather than a decision.

### Close-out

The cycle's last commit is generally bookkeeping and its body describes that bookkeeping:

1. Acceptance check: run the check the opening stated and record what it showed, pass or fail.
   A check that failed is a finding, and why it failed is determined.
2. Finalize:
   - sync the title if the scope shifted (and every anchor back-reference)
   - replace the provisional solution statement with what was done, drop the
     `(current)` / `(done)` markers
   - add any design subsections the deliberation grew, and complete the closing rung's subsection
3. Move and record: move the block into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
   - which creates the section ([Chores sections](#chores-sections))
   - add the title-only `## Table of Contents` entry
   - write the `## Done` entry ([The close-out move][tcm])
4. Validate: full validation and update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
5. Close-out shape: choose the shape with the user and record the choice in the closing
   rung's subsection ([Close-out shapes](agent-data/jj.md#close-out-shapes)). Nothing reshapes

   - fast-forward `main`, before which the cycle is not permanent
   - install the artifact
   - delete the bookmark, locally and remotely (hard rule 13)
7. Backfill: done at the next opening's step 1.

content.content:
### The close-out move

The chores section is created at close-out by moving the `## In Progress` block
([Chores sections](../AGENTS.md#chores-sections)), four transforms and no rewriting:

- **Heading levels shift so the title becomes the section's `##`**, the items shifting with it.
  Anchors survive.
- **Rung refs renumber** into the destination file's `[N]` namespace
  ([Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)).
- **Repo-root-relative links gain `../`**, since the block moves into `notes/chores/`.
- **The block's forward-looking notes are rewritten**, since they described a future that has
  now happened.

Check the renumbered refs and the rebased links by hand. The `## Done` entry written at the
same time is the version, then a bold title line with its chores `[N]` ref, detail as
sub-bullets ([Done entry form](#done-entry-form)), and the `## In Progress` block is replaced
with `_No cycle currently in progress._`. Under a program heading this retires the cycle's
block only: the program heading and its ladder stay, the shipped rung flipped `(done)`.

### Chores commit references
=== chores conventions ===
## Chores conventions

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the cycle title

## Advancing X.Y.Z: patch by default

Which of the three numbers moves is not a classification problem
([why](rationale.md#advancing-xyz-patch-by-default)): **patch by default, minor by the user's
call, major by the project's promise.**

- **Patch by default**: every cycle advances `Z`, whatever it touched. Code or docs, large or
  small, none of it matters, so the choice costs no deliberation.
- **Minor is deliberate and rare**: the user names it at a cycle's opening when the change
  deserves a visible marker in the history, and the agent never infers it from a change's
  content or size.
- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
  users. A project that makes that promise records it as its local edit of this rule, and
  absent one the default above governs.

## Grammar and storage

One spelling everywhere the version is written:

```
<public>[-<suffix>]
```

- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.

## Reference numbering

Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.

Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
file's number. To cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code

## docs: fix dev artifacts

### Problem

The agent-files leave six cycle-protocol gaps that this cycle met in one sitting, each a rule
the tightening either never placed or left one link short.

* The single-name convention says a cycle builds as `vc-x1-dev` and `main` as `vc-x1`, but no
  agent-file places the rename at a cycle beat, and two closings landed still named
  `vc-x1-dev`.
* The close-out shape list lost its link to the trapezoid recipe in the tightening, and the
  shapes read in a different order in AGENTS.md and jj.md.
* The per-rung flow's describe step reaches the commit-body form only at one remove, which let
  a description get drafted in the retired two-paragraph form.
* The Cycle term names single-step and multi-step without saying how to choose, which is how
  this cycle began as edits on `main`.
* The commit-body form lets a top-level `-` stand with no `*` above it, which reads as a
  solution to nothing, and it says nothing about a bookend commit, whose body has no problem
  to state.
* Close-out shapes names the three shapes without saying how to look at the net change before
  choosing one.

### Solution

The rename is named as an Opening step of its own and the restore as a step of the trapezoid
recipe, the recipe is relinked from the close-out shape list, the commit-body form is cued at
the describe step, the Cycle term says when a cycle is single-step or multi-step, the
commit-body form pairs every solution under a problem and makes a bookend body a pointer to
the record, and Close-out shapes says how to preview a squash before choosing.

- `grep -n '^name = ' Cargo.toml` reads `vc-x1-dev` on every rung of the bookmark and `vc-x1`

  restores the name
- every link added resolves: Close-out step 5 to the recipe, Opening step 6 and recipe step 2

## docs: reshape at land

### Problem

The close-out builds the trapezoid, restores the plain name, and moves the published bookmark
sideways before the review that landing exists for, so a review finding costs sideways pushes of
published history. Three nearby gaps ride along: the at-rest contract does not name a
`jj git push` landing as a push, the version scheme's shape-versus-contents test is undecidable
in practice, and the close-out shape choice lacks the gitk views that show the net change at
full context.

and records the shape, put landing pushes under the at-rest contract, simplify Advancing X.Y.Z
to patch by default with minor deliberate and rare, and add a jj.md section on reading a change
in gitk at full context, pointed at from README.md.

content.text:
Agreed, and the numbers say why. The net diff is 15 files, 525 insertions and 443 deletions, spread over six of the agent-files plus three notes files. There is no single thing a squash body could name: "advance patch by default" and "read a change in gitk at full context" share no text, no file, and no reader. A squash would need four `*` facets that do not decompose one problem, which prose.md's commit-body form says is a body "asking to be more than one commit."

**The sharpest tell is the two rungs you inserted mid-cycle.** `docs: empty custom.md into the agent-files` deletes `notes/dogfood.md`, 168 lines, and shrinks `custom.md` to its shell. That is a findable event. Someone asking later when the dogfood log retired wants `git log --grep dogfood` to land on that commit, not on a 525-line squash called "reshape at land". Same for the Terminology deletions.

**But the real argument is that the trapezoid gives both readings at once**, so it is not a tradeoff. `git log --first-parent main` shows one commit per cycle, exactly the trunk legibility squash is chosen for, while every rung stays reachable underneath. Squash only wins when the rungs are scaffolding nobody will want to look at again. These are six independently meaningful rule changes.

**And this cycle in particular should not lose its seams.** It rewrote the landing rule itself, so its own history is the primary evidence for whether the new order works. The fifth acceptance-check item literally reports on this landing. Collapsing the ladder would erase the record at the one place the record is the point.

Worth noting the choice was really trapezoid against squash, not three ways: keep-separate also preserves the rungs, but it puts all seven on `main`'s first-parent line, which is the thing the trapezoid exists to prevent. You tested the right alternative.

## Trapezoid close-out recipe

The reshape behind the trapezoid shape, run at [Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)
step 2: the close-out commit, pushed linearly by the closing rung, becomes a merge whose
first parent is the trunk line and whose second parent is the cycle's ladder. Nothing here
publishes, the merge goes out with Land's fast-forward.

```
  main line   ...--<base>------------------<closeout>--
                      \                    /
  ladder             <rung-1>--...--<tip>-+
```

- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle
  opened. It becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a cycle landed
  linearly since (squash or keep-separate shape) sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, reshaped here.

1. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge.
   Parent order is the argument order.
2. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on
   its own. What step 1 leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r` re-parents
   descendants onto the rebased commit's old parent, so the empty `@` lands beside the merge
   on `<tip>` and the tree reverts to pre-close-out content, which looks alarming and is not.
3. Verify two parents: `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'`
   must list both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>` is an ancestor of
   `<tip>` (observed at three consecutive close-outs), but a collapsed merge is
   indistinguishable from a correct one in `jj log --no-graph`.

Details:

- **Trailers survive.** The restore's squash and the reshape change `<closeout>`'s SHA but
  not its change id, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped at the closing push stay valid in both
  directions.
- **Immutability.** No flag is needed: a topic bookmark's commits are not on `trunk()` until
  Land's fast-forward.

Recovery:

- **Nothing is published until Land's fast-forward**, so the whole reshape is undoable with
  `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge**: undo and redo step 1 with the corrected revisions.
  Do not land a shape you did not intend. After the fast-forward the remote boundary is
  crossed and recovery is forward-only.
- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 2 skipped): `jj new <closeout>` after the
  fact. Any commit made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a rebase onto the
  merge.

## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
  install dir with stale binaries.
- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
  flow's install.

**Single-name variant**: a repo striving to release makes the package name the binary's name,
plain `<name>` on `main` only:

- **The opening renames**: its bump sets `<name>-dev` beside the suffixed version, and every
  rung and the closing build under the dev name, the closing over the bare version.
- **Land restores**: the rename back to `<name>` is Land's act, so the stable name is only
  ever installed from what `main` will carry.
- **A build script guards the pairing** on every cargo verb: a suffixed version under the
  stable name fails the build, so no mid-cycle install can clobber the consumers' binary.
